To determine the number of good subsets of the set \(\{1, 2, 3, \ldots, 13\}\), we define a good subset as one where any two distinct elements \(x\) and \(y\) satisfy \(|x - y| \geq 3\). We denote \(a_n\) as the number of good subsets of the set \(\{1, 2, 3, \ldots, n\}\).

We derive a recurrence relation for \(a_n\). Considering whether the element \(n\) is included or not, we have:
- If \(n\) is not included, the number of good subsets is \(a_{n-1}\).
- If \(n\) is included, then \(n-1\) and \(n-2\) cannot be included, leading to the number of good subsets being \(a_{n-3}\).

Thus, the recurrence relation is:
\[ a_n = a_{n-1} + a_{n-3} \]

The base cases are:
- \(a_0 = 1\) (the empty set)
- \(a_1 = 2\) (subsets: \(\{\}, \{1\}\))
- \(a_2 = 3\) (subsets: \(\{\}, \{1\}, \{2\}\))

Using the recurrence relation, we compute the values step by step:
\[
\begin{align*}
a_3 & = a_2 + a_0 = 3 + 1 = 4, \\
a_4 & = a_3 + a_1 = 4 + 2 = 6, \\
a_5 & = a_4 + a_2 = 6 + 3 = 9, \\
a_6 & = a_5 + a_3 = 9 + 4 = 13, \\
a_7 & = a_6 + a_4 = 13 + 6 = 19, \\
a_8 & = a_7 + a_5 = 19 + 9 = 28, \\
a_9 & = a_8 + a_6 = 28 + 13 = 41, \\
a_{10} & = a_9 + a_7 = 41 + 19 = 60, \\
a_{11} & = a_{10} + a_8 = 60 + 28 = 88, \\
a_{12} & = a_{11} + a_9 = 88 + 41 = 129, \\
a_{13} & = a_{12} + a_{10} = 129 + 60 = 189.
\end{align*}
\]

Thus, the number of good subsets of \(\{1, 2, 3, \ldots, 13\}\) is \(\boxed{189}\).
